transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

I keep forgetting everyday things—appointments, errands, even important family plans—and it’s starting to cause problems at home. I used to be able to keep track of everything, but lately, things are just slipping through the cracks and causing tension with my husband.
How long have you been noticing these memory issues, and have you also been feeling down, depressed, or unusually anxious lately?

These issues have been really disruptive for about a year and a half, ever since I scaled back my consulting work, though I've actually had milder versions of these focus struggles since I was a kid in elementary school. I don't feel depressed or unusually anxious, just very frustrated with myself because of the tension it's causing at home.
Are you still able to manage your daily responsibilities, like handling finances, driving, or taking medications, completely on your own, or do you now need help with these tasks?

I technically still do these things on my own, but I struggle a lot and it's causing a lot of strain. For instance, I'll get distracted and leave bills or financial paperwork, like our mortgage refinancing, half-finished on my desk for weeks. Because of this constant forgetfulness, my husband feels like he can't rely on me to handle our family logistics anymore.
Have you recently been diagnosed with any medical or neurological conditions, or did you experience any head injuries around the time these symptoms worsened?

No, I haven't had any head injuries or been diagnosed with any other medical or neurological conditions. The changes really just seemed to happen after I transitioned away from my structured consulting work and lost that daily routine.
Could you tell me more about the focus struggles you had during elementary school? For example, did you often get easily distracted, lose your belongings, or struggle to finish schoolwork back then?

Yes, back in elementary school, my teachers often wrote on my report cards that I was bright but constantly daydreaming, chatting, and forgetting to turn in homework I'd actually finished. My parents also used to joke that I was always "off in my own world" instead of doing my chores.
Have you experienced any physical symptoms like chronic fatigue, sleep changes, or hormonal shifts (such as menopause) around the same time these memory issues became more noticeable?

No, I haven't really noticed any chronic fatigue, sleep changes, or hormonal shifts like menopause. Those kinds of physical symptoms don't seem to be a factor for me at all. It really just feels like a struggle with my focus and keeping things organized.
Along with these focus and organization struggles, do you often feel internally restless, have trouble sitting still, or find yourself acting or speaking impulsively?

Yes, absolutely—if I have to sit still for too long, I get this pent-up, "itchy" feeling and end up constantly bouncing my leg or tapping my pen. I also struggle with speaking impulsively, often blurting out ideas and accidentally interrupting or talking over others before they can finish their sentences.

These symptoms cause significant impairment in her daily life and relationships, and other potential causes (such as mood disorders, sleep disorders, menopause, or head trauma) have been ruled out. Therefore, F90.0 (Disturbance of activity and attention) remains the primary and final diagnosis.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a long-standing history of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity dating back to elementary school (prior to age 12), meeting the criteria for Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), combined presentation (ICD-10: F90.0). She exhibits significant inattentive symptoms (forgetfulness, difficulty sustaining attention on administrative tasks, poor organization) and hyperactive/impulsive symptoms (internal restlessness, fidgeting, blurting out, and interrupting others). These symptoms cause substantial functional impairment in her marital relationship and daily logistics, and have become more prominent following a loss of structured routine. Other psychiatric, medical, and neurological conditions have been ruled out.
